title: Scoring Guide – IS3513
headerSubtitle: CVSS, the Risk Matrix, and Why the Two Don’t Always Agree

sections.html: You’ve finished Lab 5.1. You have your top 10 vulnerabilities on LoneStar DevOps — now you’re staring at the Findings and Risk Analysis sections wondering how to turn “I found a thing” into a defensible score. Here’s the one idea to hold onto: every finding gets two different numbers, and they answer two different questions. Most of the confusion comes from treating them as the same number. They’re not.

sections.label: The Two Scores You’re Producing
paragraphs: CVSS doesn’t know anything about LoneStar. It doesn’t know they’re prepping a Series B, doesn’t know the MySQL box holds every customer’s credentials, doesn’t know the portal can’t go offline during business hours. That context-free consistency is its strength — an analyst in San Antonio and a vendor in Berlin score the same bug the same way. The risk score is the opposite: it exists entirely to bring LoneStar’s context back in. A scanner can hand you CVSS. Only you can tell Amanda what it means for her.

ScoreWhat it measuresWhere it lives
CVSS base scoreHow dangerous the vulnerability is in the abstract — regardless of who owns the system. A standardized, client-independent number.Severity rating on each Finding
Risk score (Likelihood × Impact)How much the vulnerability actually threatens LoneStar specifically, given their business, assets, and exposure.Risk Analysis section & 5×5 matrix

sections.label: The whole point:
sections.html: When these two scores disagree, that disagreement is the most valuable thing in your report. A high-CVSS bug on a throwaway asset and a mid-CVSS bug on the crown jewels is exactly the judgment a client pays a consultant for. Part 3 is where that pays off.

sections.label: Part 1 · CVSS 3.1 — Scoring the Vulnerability Itself
paragraphs: Score every finding with the official FIRST CVSS 3.1 calculator: first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1. There are two ways to get a score. If the CVE already has one — most of your WordPress, Apache, PHP, and dependency findings will — look it up on the NVD and read its published 3.1 vector, but still understand why each metric was set that way, because you’ll defend it to the client. {w('If there is no single CVE')} — default credentials, a former employee’s account left active, a misconfiguration — you walk the calculator yourself from the vulnerability’s real characteristics.
sections.tip: Pitfall: a lot of older CVE entries show a CVSS 2.0 score, which doesn’t line up with 3.1. Always score on the 3.1 calculator so the whole class is comparable.

sections.label: The Eight Base Metrics, in Plain Language
paragraphs: You’re answering eight small, concrete questions. Don’t overthink them.
items: Attack Vector (AV) — where must the attacker be? Network → Adjacent → Local → Physical. Closer required = lower score.
Attack Complexity (AC) — how hard is the exploit, beyond the attacker’s control? Low = fire it off reliably; High = needs a race condition or special setup.
Privileges Required (PR) — what access do they need first? None / Low / High. Default credentials are the classic PR:None — the door’s already unlocked.
User Interaction (UI) — does a victim have to do something (click a link)? None, or Required. Required lowers the score.
Scope (S) — can the blast escape its own security boundary? Unchanged, or Changed. Scope:Changed is the single biggest score multiplier — use it carefully.
Confidentiality / Integrity / Availability (C / I / A) — what does a successful attack cost? None / Low / High each. Read data = C, alter data = I, take it down = A.
sections.tip: The classic mix-up: Attack Vector is where the attacker stands; Attack Complexity is how hard the exploit is once they’re there. Different axes.

sections.label: From Score to Severity
paragraphs: The calculator returns a number from 0.0 to 10.0, which maps to the severity label you write on the Finding. These are the official FIRST CVSS 3.1 bands:

CVSS base scoreSeverity
9.0 – 10.0Critical
7.0 – 8.9High
4.0 – 6.9Medium
0.1 – 3.9Low
0.0None / Informational

Carry two things into the report for every finding. First, the vector string the calculator produces — it’s the receipt that lets anyone reconstruct your number. Second, one sentence of rationale for why you set the metrics that way. A score with no explanation is just a number, and a number nobody can defend is worth nothing to a client.

sections.label: Worked Example — the Mechanics
paragraphs: Say you found an unauthenticated remote code execution on a service reachable over the network, no special conditions, no victim action, that fully compromises the box. Walk the metrics: AV Network, AC Low, PR None, UI None, Scope Unchanged, C/I/A High/High/High.
sections.tip: That’s the textbook worst case. Every one of your findings is a step down from it — an attacker who needs local access first (AV:L), a bug that only leaks data (I:N), a flaw that needs a click (UI:R). Move the metrics to match reality and let the calculator do the arithmetic.

sections.label: Part 2 · The 5×5 Risk Matrix — Scoring the Risk to LoneStar
paragraphs: Now switch hats — CVSS is done. You’re building a 5×5 grid: every finding gets a Likelihood (1–5) and an Impact (1–5), and Risk = Likelihood × Impact. This is where LoneStar’s world comes back into the picture.
Likelihood — how probable is exploitation, here?

12345
RareUnlikelyPossibleLikelyAlmost Certain

Reason it out: Is the thing exposed to the internet or buried on an internal segment? Does working exploit code already exist? Does the attacker need credentials or local access first (which lowers likelihood)? Is it something bots scan for around the clock — default creds, exposed admin panels are Likely-to-Almost-Certain.
Impact — what does it cost LoneStar if it happens?

12345
NegligibleMinorModerateMajorCatastrophic
Here you must think in LoneStar’s specifics, not generic severity.
items: $12M ARR, 200+ customers, Series B in due diligence. A breach that surfaces during investor due diligence doesn’t just cost data — it can cost the round.
Customer credentials and API keys live in the database. Anything touching that asset is a candidate for Major or Catastrophic — the blast radius is every customer.
The customer portal is the business. Availability hits there are far worse than the same downtime on an internal dev box.
sections.tip: Two findings with identical CVSS can land on completely different Impact rows purely because of which asset they touch. That’s correct — that’s the point of the section.

sections.label: Risk Score and Bands
paragraphs: Multiply Likelihood by Impact, then color-code onto the grid:

Risk = Likelihood × ImpactBand
15 – 25Critical
10 – 14High
5 – 9Medium
1 – 4Low

Plot all 10 findings on the 5×5 grid. That visual is what Amanda actually reads — executives grasp “top-right red quadrant” far faster than “CVSS 9.8.” Translating the technical into the visual-and-business is the whole job of this section.

sections.label: Part 3 · CVSS ≠ Business Priority
paragraphs: Here’s the payoff of producing two scores instead of one. They will sometimes disagree, and when they do, business risk wins — as long as you explain why. The CVSS numbers below are illustrative (yours come from your own calculator runs), but the reasoning is exactly what your report has to show:

FindingCVSS (illustrative)Real priorityWhy they diverge
MySQL default root credentials~7.3 (High)HighestLower CVSS, but it exposes every customer’s data — the crown-jewel asset for a company in Series B due diligence.
WordPress SQL injection9.8 (Critical)High, not topHuge CVSS, but it sits on the public marketing / WordPress surface, not the customer data store.
Apache privilege-escalation CVE~7.8 (High)MediumDangerous once you are already on the box — needs local access first, so real-world likelihood is lower.
SSH weak passwords~8.8 (High)HighAdministrative-access risk — crackable credentials on accounts that can touch production.

Look at the top two rows: the vulnerability with the lower CVSS is the higher business priority. Rank purely by CVSS and you’d hand Amanda a report that puts the marketing-site bug above the one that leaks her entire customer base — and she’d be right to fire NEXUS over it.
items: A high CVSS on a low-value or isolated asset is lower business risk than the raw number suggests (public WordPress SQLi).
A moderate CVSS on the crown-jewel asset is higher business risk than the raw number suggests (MySQL default creds on the customer database).
What’s reachable from the internet, what data an asset holds, and what breaks if it’s compromised all move business risk up or down independently of CVSS.
sections.tip: Priority isn’t only about risk — it’s about what LoneStar can do. When you sequence remediation, weigh remediation complexity and their real constraints: a 2-person DevOps team (Sarah and Miguel), no staging environment, a zero-downtime customer portal, and a 4-week window before the enterprise review. Lead with quick wins (disable the former-employee account, change the default MySQL password, rotate exposed API keys) so Sarah has something to show Amanda next unit.

sections.label: Before You Export — Make Your Scores Agree With Themselves
paragraphs: Your two scores are allowed to point different directions — that’s Part 3 — but they have to be internally consistent and explained. This is the easiest way to throw away points you already earned:
items: The severity label on a Finding must match the CVSS score you gave it. Don’t call something “Critical” in Findings and score it 6.4.
Your Risk Analysis rating may differ from raw CVSS — but only if you say why, in LoneStar’s terms. That “why” is the entire section.
The single most common way to lose Risk Analysis points is a uniform “high risk” on all ten findings with no reasoning. Differentiate them — each finding gets its own “so what?” for Amanda.
A given finding must carry the same severity everywhere it appears — Findings, Risk Analysis, and Executive Summary. Ratings that drift between sections read as carelessness.

sections.label: The bar:
sections.html: A report where every finding has a defensible CVSS vector, a differentiated likelihood-and-impact reasoned through LoneStar’s business, and a priority order that reflects business risk rather than raw CVSS — that’s the actual job of a security consultant. That’s what Lab 5.2 is testing.

sections.label: Quick Reference
items: CVSS 3.1 bands: 9.0–10.0 Critical · 7.0–8.9 High · 4.0–6.9 Medium · 0.1–3.9 Low · 0.0 None/Informational
Likelihood (1–5): Rare · Unlikely · Possible · Likely · Almost Certain
Impact (1–5): Negligible · Minor · Moderate · Major · Catastrophic
Risk = Likelihood × Impact: 15–25 Critical · 10–14 High · 5–9 Medium · 1–4 Low
